content.thinking:
I need to pin down the actual symptom for the postmortem—purchases were being filed as "General" instead of their proper category, which shows up as a drop in the share of purchases categorized confidently. I should word this carefully to reflect what users actually observed.

Now I'm building the causal chain: the symptom traces back to the categoriser running model v2 on all replicas instead of v1, which I can tie to the deploy event and the metrics confirming all three replicas were on the new revision. I need to rule out the earlier deploy as the cause by checking that the service was healthy on metrics between that deploy and the actual onset time.

For the mechanism, F1 explains that v2's vocabulary is lowercase-only but the categoriser doesn't lowercase input before splitting the title, so capitalized words fail to match and fall back to an unconfident General category — I'll cite F1 for this without re-running it, and keep the final step of the chain to one sentence, leaving deeper mechanism explanation for the root cause section.

Putting this in plain words: moving to the newer categorising model likely left many titles with capital letters unrecognised, since the model expects lowercase and the shop doesn't lowercase before passing titles in. I'm also noting the risk that reverting to v2 before a real fix would bring the same failure right back, and flagging as a contributing factor that there's no evidence anyone tested v2 against capitalised titles before the rollout.

I should propose adding a pre-deploy check that runs each categoriser model against a representative set of real titles, including capitalised ones, comparing confidence share against the current model before any model change can merge. A second contributing factor is that the rollout hit all replicas at once with no canary or staged release that could have caught the confidence drop and limited the blast radius.

For CF-3, I'm weighing whether the missing page counts as a real factor — since Argus mitigated quickly anyway, paging probably wouldn't have shortened the incident, so it's more of a standalone finding than a root cause.

F1's claim about code living in two places is a root cause, not a factor. For action items, I'm drafting a pre-merge check comparing a new categoriser model against real purchase titles to catch confidence drops before deployment, plus a canary rollout with automatic rollback tied to confident-share monitoring.

Then there's the process gap: linking CategorisationConfidenceLow to an on-call rotation so alerts actually page someone. I'm also checking whether revision 7c3ca00c's categorising.py matches main — D1 only confirms files are unchanged from d268 to 7c3c, not whether main matches 7c3c, so I need to be careful not to assume that connection.

I could add an action item to verify categorising.py at 7c3ca00c against main before relying on PR #406, and separately, since F1's reasoning is untested, run the proposed test against 7c3ca00c's code to confirm the mechanism actually causes the bug.

Now I'm reviewing what went well: Argus pinpointed the onset and linked it to the P2 deploy via the diff around T11/T12, the Mitigation Agent rolled back at T17, Argus ruled out flag changes by checking provider history at T14, and Code-Fix drafted PR #406 with a test.

For what went wrong, nobody paged and the logs went unread at T13, though there isn't much else to flag. Nothing stands out as a lucky break here—the deploy's config-scoped fault made rollback effective, but that's not really luck, so I'll leave that section empty. I also want to note the key assumptions: Code-Fix's fix assumes the main branch's categorising.py matches revision 7c3ca00c, that the deploy only touched the values file per D1, and that the rollback correctly restored revision d268103.

Since the record doesn't explicitly state which revision the rollback targeted, I should rely instead on the solid metrics from T5—series_before looks healthy across the 360-minute window before 21:33, which covers P1 at 17:27. That's a dependable data point to cite alongside T6, avoiding reliance on shakier assumptions about P1's resolution.

I'll be careful to avoid stating raw numbers directly, using placeholder references like {T10.2} for replica counts and {T10.1} for timestamps instead, while names like "v1", "v2", and "categoriser.model" are fine to use plainly.

For the actual steps: first, that purchases stopped being confidently categorised from the onset—the confident-categorisation share dropped well below normal while failed requests stayed within typical variation, citing AL1, T5, T6 without any impact figures. Second, that the categoriser switched to model v2 instead of v1 because the deploy at {P2.1} changed only that one setting in the production values file (per D1), and by {T10.1} all {T10.2} replicas were running that revision (per T10)—citing P2, D1, and T10, while ruling out the earlier P1 deploy since pre-onset metrics show things healthy with it in place, and ruling out flag changes since only Argus touched anything in the hour before, per T14.

Third, I'm noting that C2 and C1 are really the same underlying cause rather than something to rule out separately, and adding a step that model v2 likely fails to recognize the shop's capitalized titles since it was trained on lowercased text and the shop never lowercases before sending—citing F1, with the symptom summarized simply as purchases no longer being categorized confidently.

action_items.item: Add a pre-merge check for any change to categoriser.model: run the candidate model on a sample of real purchase titles in their original case, and block the change if its confident share falls below the current model's.
Roll changes to categoriser.model out to a canary first, and promote them to every replica only while the canary's confident share stays at the current level.
Route CategorisationConfidenceLow to an on-call rotation so that a person is paged when it fires.

Run the test proposed in PR #406 against the categorising code of revision 7c3ca00c7528df68d533f6e87acd4f23a55ab342, to show whether the capitalised-title mechanism Code-Fix read on main is what actually ran.

causal_chain.step: Purchases were no longer categorised confidently: from the onset, the share of purchases the shop put in a category with confidence fell well below its usual level, while failed requests rose no more than they normally vary.

ruled_out.what: The earlier deploy of revision d268103129978816ce705c50c14cd42c7c5fe46e at {P1.1}: the metrics read back show the confident share at its healthy level with that revision in place, up to the onset.
A feature-flag change: the flag provider's history shows no flag changes by anyone but Argus in the hour before {T14.4}.

causal_chain.step: The categoriser was answering with model v2 instead of v1. The deploy at {P2.1} changed categoriser.model from v1 to v2 in deploy/values-production.yaml, and that was the only file it changed (D1). As of {T10.1}, all {T10.2} replicas were running that revision (T10).

Model v2 likely fails to recognise the capitalised titles the shop sends it, because it expects words lowercased the way its training pipeline lowercased them, and the shop's code does not lowercase titles before passing them on.

input.cause_in_plain_words: Moving the shop to a newer model for sorting purchases into categories likely left product titles with capital letters unrecognised, because the new model expects lower-case words and the shop hands it titles in their original capitalisation.

contributing_factors.factor: No check was seen that ran model v2 against product titles in their original capitalisation before the move to v2 went out. Code-Fix's reading says the existing v2 tests covered only titles whose matching word was already lowercase.
contributing_factors.had_it_been_otherwise: A check comparing v2 with v1 on capitalised titles would likely have shown v2 failing to categorise them confidently, and stopped the change before it reached production.
contributing_factors.label: CF-1

contributing_factors.factor: No staged or canary rollout was seen for the model change. The deploy put the new revision on every replica, and harm began right after it.
contributing_factors.had_it_been_otherwise: A canary judged on the confident share would have exposed only part of the purchases to v2 and held the change back before it reached every replica.
contributing_factors.label: CF-2

went_well.item: The Investigator Agent tied the incident to the deploy of revision 7c3ca00c7528df68d533f6e87acd4f23a55ab342 by reading that deploy's diff, which showed that it changed only the categoriser model setting.
Argus read the flag provider's history to rule out a flag change before acting.
The Mitigation Agent rolled back the deployment of io-shop. The action can be put back.
The Code-Fix Agent proposed a shop-side fix with a test, as draft PR #406.

went_wrong: Nobody was paged: the alert was linked to no on-call incident, so no person was brought in while the incident ran.

input.root_cause: Model v2 does not lowercase words itself (its `lowercases_its_input` is False), because its vocabulary was built from titles its training pipeline had already lowercased, yet the shop's `categorise` passes `title.split()` to the model in the title's original case. Under v2, a title with no known all-lowercase word therefore misses the vocabulary and falls through to "General" marked not confident, while every request still succeeds.
input.still_at_risk: Setting categoriser.model back to v2 before a shop-side fix is running would likely bring the same fall in confident categorisation straight back, because the shop's code still passes titles to the model without lowercasing them.
input.symptom: Many purchases were no longer categorised confidently
